screens.title: Advanced Standard Library Features and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Master transforms, lambdas, remove-erase, and iterator categories for idiomatic C++

narration.text: Welcome. In this chapter we focus on the parts of the C++ Standard Library that let you manipulate collections declaratively and safely. Rather than writing manual loops to map, sum, filter, or sort, you will learn how algorithms like std::transform, std::accumulate, std::remove_if and std::sort express intent directly and tend to be more robust and readable. You will also learn how lambda expressions and simple function objects let you provide custom behavior inline, and why the lambda capture list matters for correctness and lifetime. We will walk through practical examples: squaring numbers with std::transform, computing sums with std::accumulate, sorting a list of Student or Employee objects with a custom comparator lambda, and safely removing elements using the remove-erase idiom. Along the way we will cover iterator categories and why algorithms require specific iterator capabilities, and we’ll highlight common pitfalls such as iterator invalidation and forgetting includes. By the end of this lesson you will be able to choose the right STL algorithm, write concise lambdas, and avoid common correctness and performance mistakes. Think about a data transformation you commonly write by hand — imagine replacing that loop with a single intent-revealing algorithm call.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: STL algorithms plus lambdas let you write clearer, safer, and often faster code. Learning these idioms reduces bugs and expresses intent more directly than manual loops.

Advanced Standard Library Features and Best Practices

This final chapter shows how to use advanced STL algorithms and lambdas to transform, accumulate, filter, and sort data. You’ll learn idioms that replace error-prone loops with clear, efficient calls and how iterator categories affect which algorithms you can use.

In this lesson
  • Use std::transform and std::accumulate for mapping and reduction tasks.
  • Write lambdas with correct capture semantics for predicates and operations.
  • Apply remove-erase safely and choose the right container for performance.
Transform
Map a function over a range and write to output
std::transform(src.begin(), src.end(), dst.begin(), [](int n){ return n*n; });
Accumulate
Reduce a range to a single value
long long s = std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0LL);
Explore Key Topics
Transforms
Apply operations to ranges with a single call and keep intent clear.
Lambdas
Inline function objects that capture surrounding state when needed.
Iterators
Different categories limit algorithm choices and performance.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Understand powerful algorithms, lambdas, iterator roles, and safe STL patterns

narration.text: These learning objectives guide what you will be able to do at the end of this chapter. First, you will be able to apply advanced STL algorithms for common data tasks: transforms to map values, accumulate to reduce ranges, and remove-if to filter elements. Second, you will learn to write lambda expressions and function objects to customize algorithm behavior; you will see how capture lists like by-value or by-reference change lifetime and semantics. Third, you will identify common pitfalls such as iterator invalidation, missing includes, and choosing the wrong container for an algorithm, and adopt best practices to avoid them. Finally, you will implement custom sorting and filtering using user-defined predicates and understand iterator categories so you pick algorithms compatible with your container. Each objective pairs a concrete skill with why it matters: correctness, performance, and clearer intent. Throughout you will practice with short code examples and a longer Student/Employee demo so you can apply these skills immediately.

keyIdea.title: Learning focus
keyIdea.text: Move from manual loops to algorithmic patterns that express intent, are safer, and often offer better performance.

You will apply std::transform and std::accumulate in short code snippets that illustrate data flow — what goes in, what comes out, and where results are stored. You will practice the remove-erase idiom to remove elements safely, learn to pair remove_if with erase correctly, and understand why remove_if alone does not shrink the container. You will also reason about iterator categories so you know when std::sort is appropriate and when an algorithm requires random access iterators. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Practice & Safety
What you'll practice
  • Transform & accumulate: Map values and reduce results without manual index arithmetic.
  • Remove-erase idiom: Use std::remove_if then container.erase to actually remove elements.
  • Custom sort: Provide a comparator lambda that captures nothing or only what it needs.

Quick note

Prefer std::vector unless a use case requires frequent middle insertions or stable iterators; understand erase complexity for your chosen container.

screens.title: Using std::transform and std::accumulate
screens.subtitle: Map values and compute totals without manual loops

narration.text: Let's define the claim: std::transform maps an operation across a range and writes results to an output range; std::accumulate reduces a range to a single value. Both avoid manual indexing and express intent. Consider a vector of integers you want to square and then sum. With std::transform you produce a destination vector by passing the source begin/end, a destination iterator, and a unary operation, often a lambda. Then std::accumulate takes the begin/end of the destination and an initial value to compute the sum. A concrete example: create numbers {1,2,3,4,5}, transform into squares, and accumulate with an initial zero long long. Misconception: people sometimes expect transform to modify the source in-place; it writes to the output range you pass. To modify in-place pass the same begin for output or use a range-based algorithm variant. Another common mistake is forgetting to size the destination vector — the output iterator must be valid. Practice tip: when you only need an aggregated value and not the intermediate vector, you can combine mapping into the accumulator to avoid temporaries. Takeaway: use transform to express elementwise change, and accumulate to express reduction. How would you map a non-primitive struct field instead of integers?

keyIdea.title: Transform + Accumulate
keyIdea.text: Use std::transform for elementwise mapping and std::accumulate for reductions; ensure output iterators are valid and consider combining steps when possible.

content.html:
Core Concept

Map and reduce with STL algorithms

Using std::transform and std::accumulate expresses two different data transformations: producing a new sequence, and collapsing a sequence to a value. Both are single-pass and readable.

Key Takeaway

Transform maps, accumulate reduces. Avoid forgetting to size the output range for transform.

Concrete example

Square numbers and sum them using transform then accumulate. Destination vector must match source size.

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm> // std::transform
#include <numeric>   // std::accumulate
#include <iostream>

int main() {
  std::vector<int> numbers = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
  std::vector<int> squared(numbers.size());

  // Apply lambda to each element and store in squared
  std::transform(numbers.begin(), numbers.end(), squared.begin(),
                 [](int n) { return n * n; });

  // Sum the squared numbers
  long long sum_of_squares = std::accumulate(squared.begin(), squared.end(), 0LL);

  std::cout << "Sum of squared numbers: " << sum_of_squares << std::endl;
}
Explains
  • transform applies the lambda to every element.
  • accumulate reduces to a scalar using an initial value.
Common mistake
Not sizing the destination vector or assuming remove_if removes elements physically.
Try this
Combine mapping into accumulate to avoid a temporary when you only need the sum.

screens.title: Lambda Expressions and Capture Lists
screens.subtitle: Write concise predicates and operations with correct captures

narration.text: A clear definition: a lambda expression is an anonymous function object written inline using the syntax with a capture list, parameters, optional return type, and body. Lambdas are commonly used as predicates or transformers for STL algorithms because they keep behavior close to where it is used. The capture list determines how the lambda accesses surrounding variables: empty capture means no outside variables; capture-by-value copies the variable into the lambda, while capture-by-reference lets the lambda refer to the live variable. A mixed capture like [=, &total] captures everything by value except total by reference. Concrete example: filtering a vector with a threshold variable captured by value prevents accidental modifications, whereas capturing by reference may be necessary when you want to mutate an accumulator. Misconception: capturing large objects by value can be expensive; prefer capturing references or copying only what you need. Also avoid capturing pointers to local stack objects that go out of scope. Practice: write a lambda that compares Student scores and another that captures a threshold to use with remove_if. Takeaway: choose captures that balance safety and performance, and prefer explicit captures for clarity.

keyIdea.title: Lambda capture guidance
keyIdea.text: Capture by value for safety of immutables, by reference when you need to update state—prefer explicit captures for clarity and avoid dangling references.

content.html:
Definition

Lambda structure and captures

Lambdas let you inline small function objects. Decide capture semantics deliberately: copying small values is cheap, copying large containers is not.

Example captures
// capture by value
auto f1 = [threshold](const Student &s) { return s.score < threshold; };
// capture by reference
auto f2 = [&limit](const Student &s) { return s.score < limit; };
// mixed
auto f3 = [=, &acc](const Student &s) { acc += s.score; return s.score < threshold; };
Pro tip
When a lambda outlives local scope, avoid capturing references to locals. Use copies or store state elsewhere to prevent dangling references.
Common mistake

Capturing a local variable by reference and then storing the lambda beyond the local scope creates undefined behavior when that variable goes out of scope.

Analogy

Think of capture-by-value as giving the lambda a snapshot photo; capture-by-reference is giving it a live camera feed.

Check your understanding

When would you prefer an explicit [threshold] capture over [=]? Why might you avoid [&] on a large scope?

screens.title: The Remove-Erase Idiom and std::remove_if
screens.subtitle: How to filter container elements safely and efficiently

narration.text: Claim: std::remove_if does not change a container's size; it reorders elements so undesired ones end up after a returned new logical end. You must follow remove_if with container. erase to physically remove those elements. Concrete example: given a vector of Student objects and a captured min_score_threshold, std::remove_if moves students with score below the threshold toward the end and returns an iterator to the new end. Then calling students. erase(new_end, students. end()) removes them. A common misconception is to call remove_if and assume elements are gone — iterators and size remain until erase runs. Another important detail: remove_if operates in linear time, but the complexity of erase on the container depends on container type; on vector erase can be O(N) for shifting elements, so prefer a single erase call with the returned range rather than repeatedly erasing inside a loop. Also be mindful of iterator invalidation after erase. Practice writing the remove-erase idiom and prefer stable containers or reserve capacity when performance matters. The Remove-Erase Idiom and std::remove_if means std::remove_if relocates; use container.erase(new_end, container.end()) to actually remove elements. avoid repeated single-element erase calls on vectors.. In practical terms, how to filter container elements safely and efficiently. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Remove-erase idiom
keyIdea.text: std::remove_if relocates; use container.erase(new_end, container.end()) to actually remove elements. Avoid repeated single-element erase calls on vectors.

content.html:
Process Flow

Filtering with remove_if + erase

Use remove_if to partition elements that satisfy a condition, then erase the trailing range that now contains removed elements.

Steps
  1. Call std::remove_if with a predicate lambda; capture threshold by value for safety.
  2. std::remove_if returns an iterator new_end marking valid elements.
  3. Call container.erase(new_end, container.end()) to physically remove them.
Code example
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

int min_score_threshold = 85;
auto new_end = std::remove_if(students.begin(), students.end(),
    [min_score_threshold](const Student &s) {
        return s.score < min_score_threshold;
    });
students.erase(new_end, students.end());
Pitfall

Calling erase repeatedly inside a loop on std::vector is costly. Use the single erase(new_end, end) idiom.

Why it matters

Understanding remove_if’s behavior prevents logical bugs and poor performance when removing many elements.

screens.title: Custom Sorting with std::sort and Lambdas
screens.subtitle: Define ordering using concise comparator lambdas

narration.text: Claim: std::sort sorts using random access iterators and a comparator. For custom types such as a Student struct, supply a comparator lambda that returns a Boolean indicating if the first argument comes before the second. A concrete example is sorting students by score descending: provide a lambda that compares a. score > b. score. Misconception: some learners think std::sort will accept containers like std::list; it requires random access iterators, so std::vector works but std::list does not. If you need to sort a linked structure, copy pointers into a vector, sort them, or use container-specific operations. Also avoid writing comparators that violate strict weak ordering — inconsistent comparators lead to undefined behavior. Practice: write a comparator that first compares score, then name to break ties. Performance note: std::sort is O(N log N) on average for random access containers. Takeaway: write clear comparator lambdas, ensure they form a consistent ordering, and choose a container that matches the algorithm’s iterator requirements. Custom Sorting with std::sort and Lambdas means use std::sort with comparator lambdas on random access containers. ensure comparator logic is consistent and avoids undefined behavior.. In practical terms, define ordering using concise comparator lambdas. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Sorting guidance
keyIdea.text: Use std::sort with comparator lambdas on random access containers. Ensure comparator logic is consistent and avoids undefined behavior.

content.html:
Comparison

Sort students with a comparator lambda

Write a comparator that returns true when the first element should appear before the second. For tie-breakers, include additional fields like name.

Example comparator
std::sort(students.begin(), students.end(),
  [](const Student &a, const Student &b) {
    if (a.score != b.score) return a.score > b.score; // descending
    return a.name < b.name; // tie-breaker: name ascending
  });
Common mistake

Providing an inconsistent comparator (not transitive) can make std::sort misbehave or crash. Always ensure strict weak ordering.

Why random access matters

std::sort needs to jump around the range, so containers that offer random access iterators like std::vector are required. std::list provides only bidirectional iterators.

Try this

If you must sort a std::list, consider copying elements to a vector of pointers, sorting that, or using list::sort which is optimized for lists.

Check your understanding

Write a comparator that sorts by department, then descending salary, then name.

screens.title: Iterator Categories and Algorithm Requirements
screens.subtitle: Match algorithms to iterator capabilities for correctness and performance

narration.text: Definition and reason: iterators are classified by capability — input, output, forward, bidirectional, and random access — and algorithms indicate the minimum category they require. Input iterators can read and move forward; output iterators write and move forward. Forward iterators can read and write while moving forward. Bidirectional iterators also move backward. Random access iterators can jump directly to any element. A concrete example: std::sort requires random access iterators because its implementation needs to index and swap elements arbitrarily; attempting to use it on a container that supplies only bidirectional iterators will fail. Misconception: some learners assume all iterators offer the same performance — they do not. For instance, erasing many elements from a vector may shift elements and be O(N) per erase, whereas a list can remove elements in O(1) when given an iterator, but lists cannot be sorted with std::sort efficiently. Practical guidance: pick std::vector for general-purpose sequences and performance with algorithms, reserve capacity to avoid reallocations that invalidate iterators, and consult algorithm documentation for iterator requirements. Takeaway: understanding iterator categories helps you choose both container and algorithm wisely.

keyIdea.title: Iterators matter
keyIdea.text: Algorithms require specific iterator features. Choose containers whose iterators satisfy algorithm requirements to avoid compile errors and poor runtime performance.

content.html:
Definition

Iterator categories at a glance

Input
Read forward only (e.g., stream iterators).
Bidirectional
Read/write and move both directions (e.g., std::list).
Random Access
Jump to any element quickly (e.g., std::vector, pointers).
Example

std::sort requires random access. std::remove_if only needs forward iterators. Knowing these requirements prevents compile-time errors and performance surprises.

Performance note

Vector is often the best default for algorithm work. Reserve capacity to avoid reallocations that invalidate iterators used elsewhere.

Common mistake

Trying to run std::sort on a std::list will either not compile or produce suboptimal code. Match container to algorithm.

Check

Which iterator category does your container provide, and which algorithms require that category?

screens.title: Iterator Invalidation and Safe Patterns
screens.subtitle: Why changing a container while iterating can break your program, and how to do it safely

narration.text: Iterator invalidation happens when an iterator or pointer refers to an element that has been moved or removed by a container operation. In practice this means that code which looks correct can suddenly lead to undefined behavior if you add, erase, or reallocate the container while iterating. A common example is erasing elements from a dynamic array-like container in a for loop that advances an index or iterator incorrectly. The safe patterns you should rely on are: use the erase return value when erasing by iterator so you get a valid next iterator; use the remove-erase idiom when you want to filter by predicate; or build a new container using algorithms when that is simpler and clearer. Consider also the performance implication: many single-element erases on a vector are O(N) each and can easily become quadratic, so prefer a single pass algorithm. As a concrete example, if you need to drop elements that match a condition, use an algorithm that compacts the valid elements first, then erase the trailing range. A common misconception is that iterators always stay valid after modifications. That is false — validity rules differ by container and operation. Your takeaway: know the container's invalidation rules, prefer algorithmic patterns that avoid per-element erases, and when necessary use the iterator returned by erase to continue safely. What will you check first: the container type or the erase pattern?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Modifying a container while iterating can invalidate iterators; use erase-return-value, remove-erase, or rebuild approaches to stay safe and efficient.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Iterator Invalidation
Why iterator invalidation matters

Iterators can become invalid after operations like insert, erase, or reallocation. The exact rules depend on the container. Use safe idioms to avoid undefined behavior and costly mistakes.

  • Vector: inserting or erasing may reallocate or shift elements, invalidating iterators.
  • List: erasing an element invalidates only iterators to that element; others remain valid.
  • Map/Set: erasure invalidates only iterators to erased nodes; most iterators remain valid.
Safe pattern
When erasing during iteration, use the iterator returned by erase or apply remove-erase. This avoids stepping on invalid iterators and keeps complexity predictable.
Key Takeaway

Always consult the container's invalidation rules. Prefer algorithms that transform or compact, then erase once.

Wrong vs Correct
Code example
Unsafe: erase while iterating
<!-- Unsafe: increments invalidated iterator -->
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>

int main(){
  std::vector<int> v = {1,2,3,4};
  for(auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ++it){
    if(*it % 2 == 0){
      v.erase(it); // UB: iterator 'it' becomes invalid
    }
  }
}
Safe: use erase return value
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>

int main(){
  std::vector<int> v = {1,2,3,4};
  for(auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ){
    if(*it % 2 == 0){
      it = v.erase(it); // erase returns next valid iterator
    } else {
      ++it;
    }
  }
}
Example scenario

Removing inactive user IDs from a vector of IDs during a cleanup pass. Use erase-return-value or build a new vector with std::copy_if for safety and performance.

Pitfall to avoid

Calling single-element erase repeatedly inside a loop on a vector can be O(N²). Prefer a single compacting algorithm or one-pass erase-return-value pattern.

screens.title: Choosing the Right Container
screens.subtitle: How container choice affects correctness, safety, and performance

narration.text: Choosing the right container is one of the most practical performance and correctness decisions you make in C++. Containers differ in complexity, iterator guarantees, and typical use cases. std.. vector is a strong default: it offers contiguous storage, random access iterators, and excellent cache performance. It excels when you need fast indexed access and iteration. std.. list gives stable iterators when inserting or erasing in the middle, but it pays for that with poor locality and no random access. Associative containers such as std.. map or std.. set maintain order and provide logarithmic lookup; std.. unordered underscore map provides average constant-time lookup using hashing. The practical rule: favor std.. vector unless you have a clear reason for another container. For example, heavy mid-list insertions or splice operations are good reasons to choose a list. A common misconception is to choose std.. list for delete-heavy code without measuring; often std.. vector plus algorithms or indices is faster. Also remember algorithm requirements: some algorithms, like sorting, require random access iterators and therefore cannot run on a std.. list. When performance matters, look at algorithmic complexity, iterator category, and memory behavior together. Finally, write a small benchmark or reason through complexity to confirm your choice.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Container choice should be guided by required operations, iterator category needs, and performance characteristics—`std::vector` is a good default.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Container Choice
Compare common containers
std::vector

Contiguous, random access, best for iteration and sorting. Resize may reallocate and invalidate iterators.

Typical complexity: push_back amortized O(1), random access O(1), insert/erase middle O(N)
std::list

Doubly-linked, stable iterators except for erased nodes, good for frequent middle insert/erase but poor cache locality.

Typical complexity: insert/erase O(1) given iterator, no random access
std::map / std::set

Ordered associative containers with logarithmic lookup and stable iterators to non-erased elements.

std::unordered_map

Hash-based lookup with average constant-time access; iteration order is unspecified.

Practical guidance
  • Start with std::vector. It fits many workflows and works well with algorithms.
  • Choose std::list only when you need O(1) splice or guaranteed iterator stability during middle operations.
  • Use associative containers for keyed access and when order or uniqueness matters.
  • Remember: some algorithms require random access iterators, so container choice can disallow certain algorithms.
Quick Decision Matrix
If you need fast indexed access, sorting, or compact storage — choose vector. If you need stable iterators during frequent mid-list modifications — consider list. For key-value lookup, pick map or unordered_map depending on ordered vs hashed needs.
Why it matters

Right container selection prevents incorrect algorithm choices, reduces surprises from iterator requirements, and improves performance without premature optimization.

screens.title: const Correctness and Efficient Iteration
screens.subtitle: Avoid unnecessary copies and make intent explicit with const references

narration.text: Const correctness and choosing how you iterate are small changes that have a big impact on safety and performance. When you iterate over a container and do not need to modify elements, prefer using a const reference — for example, const auto& — instead of making a copy. Copies of large objects can be expensive and unintentional mutations can hide bugs. Using const references also communicates intent to readers and enables potential optimizations. A concrete example: iterating over a vector of strings and printing them. If you use auto without reference, each element is copied on every iteration. Using const auto& avoids the copy. Another important detail: when you need to mutate elements, use a non-const reference, but be mindful of iterator invalidation rules when modifying a container's structure. A common misconception is that const slows code; in practice it often helps the compiler and prevents unintended changes. Also prefer range-based for loops for clarity unless you need indices or explicit iterators. When writing algorithms like accumulate, take care to select the right initial type and avoid narrowing. The practical habit to adopt: prefer const auto& for read-only iteration, use explicit types for accumulate when needed, and favor clarity with explicit const correctness in function parameters.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use const references for read-only iteration to avoid copies, express intent, and improve performance and safety.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Const Correctness
Why prefer const references?

Copies can be expensive for large objects and may hide bugs. Const references avoid copies and signal intent that data should not be changed.

  • Use const auto&& for perfect-forwarding scenarios, but for simple loops, prefer const auto&.
  • When using algorithms like accumulate, pick an initial accumulator type that avoids overflow and implicit casts.
  • Declare function parameters as const Type& when you only read the argument.
Takeaway

Small type decisions prevent big performance surprises. Make intent explicit with const references.

Copy vs const reference
// Copies each std::string (costly)
for (auto s : words) {
  std::cout << s << '
';
}

// No copies, read-only
for (const auto& s : words) {
  std::cout << s << '
';
}
Example: accumulate with correct type
#include <numeric>
// If summing doubles, start with 0.0 to avoid integer accumulation
double total = std::accumulate(vals.begin(), vals.end(), 0.0,
  [](double sum, double v){ return sum + v; });

screens.title: Function Objects (Functors) vs Lambdas and std::for_each
screens.subtitle: When to use a stateful functor, a lambda, or std::for_each for side effects

narration.text: Function objects, often called functors, are structs or classes that define an operator call so they can be invoked like functions. Lambdas are syntactic sugar for creating function objects inline and are usually the most concise choice for short, local operations. The trade-offs center on readability, reusability, and whether you need state. Use a functor when you want to hold persistent state across calls in a typed object, or when you need to reuse the operation in multiple places. Use a lambda for concise inline predicates or transformations passed directly to algorithms. std.. for underscore each applies a callable to every element; it can be useful for side effects but does not return a transformed range. Prefer algorithms that return results or use transform when you want to create new collections. As a concrete example, a functor can maintain a running count or external resource handle; a lambda with a capture can often replace that with less boilerplate. One misconception is that lambdas are always less efficient than named functors — typically compilers optimize both similarly, but clarity and ownership of captured state matter more. Practice: when you need stateful behavior that you might test or reuse, write a named functor; for quick predicates, write a lambda. This gives you both expressiveness and maintainability.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Lambdas are compact, functors are reusable and stateful; choose based on state needs and reusability, and prefer algorithms that express intent.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Functors & Lambdas
Functor vs Lambda
Patterns

Named functors are useful when you want a callable with persistent state and clear type identity. Lambdas are concise and ideal for local predicates and short transformations.

Stateful functor example
struct SumPrinter {
  int sum = 0;
  void operator()(int v){ sum += v; std::cout << "value: " << v << '
'; }
};
// Usage: std::for_each(vec.begin(), vec.end(), SumPrinter());
Lambda with capture for the same intent
int total = 0;
std::for_each(vec.begin(), vec.end(),
  [&total](int v){ total += v; std::cout << v << '
'; });
// total is updated via captured reference
Use a captured variable for quick local state. For reusable operations, prefer a named functor to improve testability and clarity.
Misconception
Lambdas are not inherently slower. Compiler optimizations often inline or optimize both functors and lambdas similarly. Choose for clarity and ownership of state.
When to use std::for_each
`std::for_each` is convenient for side effects. If you need a transformed container use `std::transform`, and if you need a filtered view prefer copy_if or remove-erase patterns for clarity.

screens.title: Common Mistakes & Best Practices Checklist
screens.subtitle: A practical checklist to avoid bugs, inefficiency, and surprises with the STL

narration.text: This checklist collects the most frequent mistakes and the best practices to avoid them. First, always include the correct headers: algorithms like transform and remove_if come from the algorithms header, numeric operations from the numeric header, and function utilities from the functional header. Forgetting headers leads to compilation errors. Second, prefer algorithms over raw loops when a suitable algorithm exists — they express intent, reduce errors, and are often optimized. Third, be mindful of iterator invalidation when modifying containers. Use erase-return-value, remove-erase idiom, or rebuild the container to avoid undefined behavior. Fourth, avoid repeated single-element erase calls on a vector inside a loop; this can be quadratic. Fifth, use const correctness to prevent unintended modifications and reduce copying. Sixth, choose the right container: vector for contiguous storage and random access, list for splice-heavy logic, maps for keyed access. Finally, test complexity expectations and measure where performance matters. A common misconception is that writing a straightforward loop is always faster; often the STL algorithm combined with a contiguous container is both clearer and faster. To practice, review your code for these checklist items and ask: am I using the right algorithm, the right container, and respecting iterator rules? This habit catches many bugs early.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Follow a short checklist: correct headers, prefer algorithms, respect invalidation, choose proper containers, and use const correctness—measure when performance matters.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Best Practices Checklist
Checklist
  1. Include the right headers: <algorithm>, <numeric>, <functional>.
  2. Prefer STL algorithms to manual loops when available.
  3. Respect iterator invalidation rules and prefer erase-return-value or remove-erase for deletions.
  4. Use const references to avoid copies for read-only access.
  5. Pick the right container for the operations you need; measure when in doubt.
  6. Avoid repeated single-element erase on vector inside loops; prefer bulk operations.
Check your understanding

Given a vector of 10,000 elements where you will remove 40% of elements by a predicate, would you use repeated erase, remove-erase, or build a new vector with copy_if? Explain your performance reasoning.

Quick tips
  • Write clear intent: transform, accumulate, remove_if, sort — pick names that match the operation.
  • When in doubt, benchmark a real input set, not synthetic microtests.
  • Prefer explicit types in public APIs and const references for parameters you don't modify.
Common mistake

Assuming all STL algorithms have identical performance across containers. They do not — algorithm complexity often depends on iterator category.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Compact reminders of the most important library ideas

narration.text: Here are the concise ideas to carry forward. First, std::transform applies a function to each element of a range and writes results to an output range. It expresses the intent to transform data without manual loops. Second, std::accumulate computes a cumulative value across a range using an initial value and a binary operation; use an appropriate accumulator type to avoid narrowing or overflow. Third, std::remove_if reorders elements so those matching a predicate end up at the end and returns a new logical end; pair it with erase to actually remove elements. These three algorithms are foundational for compact, readable, and efficient data processing with the STL. Remember their roles: transform for mapping, accumulate for reduction, and remove_if for predicate-driven compaction. When combined with lambdas or function objects they become expressive building blocks for many data-processing tasks.

std::transform
Applies a unary operation to each element and writes results to an output range, replacing manual mapping loops.
std::accumulate
Reduces a range to a single value using an initial accumulator and a binary operation, useful for sums and folds.
std::remove_if
Partitions elements by a predicate and returns the new logical end; pair with container erase to remove elements.
Summary Takeaway

Use the STL algorithms and lambdas to express mapping, reduction, and filtering clearly. Combine them with the right container and iterator discipline for correct, fast code.

screens.subtitle: Short definitions to anchor your practice

narration.text: A few final definitions to remember. Lambda expressions are anonymous function objects defined inline; they let you capture surrounding variables by value or reference and provide concise predicates or operations for algorithms. Iterator categories classify iterators by capability: input, output, forward, bidirectional, and random access. Algorithms often require a minimum iterator category — for example, sorting needs random access iterators. The remove-erase idiom is the standard pattern to remove elements from containers: you call remove_if to reorder matching elements to the end and then erase the trailing range from the container. These concise definitions will help you choose the right algorithm and container, write correct code, and avoid common pitfalls. Reflect on which concept you will apply first in your next small project. Key Concepts means lambdas: inline predicates; iterator categories: capabilities matter; remove-erase: logical then physical removal.. In practical terms, short definitions to anchor your practice. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Lambda Expressions
Anonymous, inline function objects that capture local variables for concise predicates and operations.
Iterator Categories
Classify iterators by capability. Random access supports jumps; bidirectional supports next and prev; algorithms require certain categories.
Remove-Erase Idiom
Call remove_if to partition unwanted elements, then erase the returned trailing range to actually remove them from the container.
